source_refs.note: Topic 20.4 with Quick Check 20.7, answered (PDF 68-69). The printed equation (one methylbenzene + 2Cl2 giving both isomers + 2HCl) is given per molecule. The book's '-CO2-' is given as -COOH; the halogen tip is added for the Quick Checks. Answers need review.

blocks.text: A group already on the benzene ring affects electrophilic substitution and decides where the incoming electrophile goes (its orientation). Substituents direct the electrophile in two ways.

An ortho-para director makes the ring more reactive than benzene and sends the electrophile to the ortho (1,2) and para (1,4) positions, with a slight preference for para; the meta product is a very minor by-product. Examples are -SR, -R, -OH, -OR, -NR2 and -SH: groups that can donate electrons to the ring.

Methylbenzene is chlorinated in the ring with aluminium chloride (or aluminium bromide for bromine) or iron, at room temperature and in the absence of UV light. The methyl group is 2,4-directing, so the product is a mixture of 2-chloromethylbenzene and 4-chloromethylbenzene: C6H5CH3 + Cl2 -> CH3C6H4Cl + HCl. Bromine gives the corresponding bromo compounds. Like CH3, the OH group of phenol activates the ring, and incoming groups go to positions 2, 4 and 6.

A meta director makes the ring less reactive than benzene and sends the electrophile to the meta (1,3) position. These groups mostly withdraw electrons and destabilise the arenium intermediate. Examples are -CN, C=O groups (-CHO, -COR), -NO2 and -COOH. Nitrobenzene is chlorinated at the meta position, giving 3-chloronitrobenzene.

blocks.alt: Top: methylbenzene + Cl2 with AlCl3 and no UV light gives 2-chloromethylbenzene + 4-chloromethylbenzene + HCl; a note says CH3 pushes electrons into the ring so positions 2 and 4 react. Bottom: nitrobenzene + Cl2 with AlCl3 gives 3-chloronitrobenzene + HCl; NO2 pulls electrons out of the ring and the new group goes to position 3.
blocks.caption: Ortho-para and meta directing groups (original diagram after the book's examples).
blocks.long_description: An electron-donating group such as CH3 makes the ring more reactive and directs a new group to positions 2 and 4. An electron-withdrawing group such as NO2 makes the ring less reactive and directs a new group to position 3.

blocks.title: Halogens are a special case
blocks.text: Halogen substituents (-Cl, -Br) make the ring slightly less reactive than benzene, yet they direct new groups to the ortho and para positions. This is needed for Quick Checks 20.7 and 20.8.

blocks.prompt: Why can phenol be nitrated under milder conditions than benzene?
blocks.explanation: The OH group donates electron density (a lone pair on oxygen) into the ring, activating it, so dilute nitric acid at room temperature is enough.

blocks.prompt: How would you prepare 3-chloronitrobenzene from benzene?
blocks.explanation: First nitrate benzene (conc. HNO3 and conc. H2SO4, below about 50 C) to nitrobenzene; then chlorinate with Cl2 and AlCl3 (or FeCl3). The NO2 group directs the chlorine to the meta position. Chlorinating first would put the nitro group at 2 or 4.

blocks.prompt: Give the main products of nitrating benzaldehyde, chlorobenzene, phenol and benzoic acid.
blocks.explanation: Benzaldehyde: 3-nitrobenzaldehyde (CHO is a meta director). Chlorobenzene: 2- and 4-chloronitrobenzene, mostly 4. Phenol: 2- and 4-nitrophenol (with concentrated acid, 2,4,6-trinitrophenol). Benzoic acid: 3-nitrobenzoic acid. Each is formed with water as the other product.
